cases.abstract: DreamBooth adapts pretrained text-to-image diffusion models from three to five subject images to preserve identity while changing context and appearance. Fine-tuning pairs a rare-token identifier with the subject's class, linking instance learning to pretrained class knowledge. A prior-preservation loss uses class images generated by the frozen model to counter the tendency to replace the class with the learned instance. We provide a public 30-subject dataset and evaluation protocol, proposing DINO embedding similarity to assess subject identity alongside prompt alignment. Across 3,000 generated images, DreamBooth on Stable Diffusion improves DINO similarity from 0.569 to 0.668 and CLIP text-image similarity from 0.255 to 0.305 over Textual Inversion. User preferences likewise favor DreamBooth for identity (68% versus 22%) and prompt fidelity (81% versus 12%): these joint comparisons support retaining the subject while following changed prompts. An Imagen ablation finds less class collapse and greater diversity with prior preservation, but slightly lower subject fidelity. Applications include novel viewpoints, artistic renditions, and property changes; rare contexts, context-appearance entanglement, overfitting, and hallucinated details still limit preservation.
cases.notes: Tables 1-2 jointly test the two-part promise: subject identity and adherence to changed prompts, not identity similarity alone. Retained the public dataset/protocol and DINO evaluation contribution. Section 3 supplies the class-prior rationale; Table 3 qualifies prior preservation as reduced collapse and greater diversity at a subject-fidelity cost. Application examples and Section 4.5 do not establish invariant identity across contexts.

cases.abstract: Toolformer learns when and how to call text-based tools by treating their usefulness for predicting subsequent text as supervision. From a few demonstrations per API, a language model samples and executes calls, retaining responses only when they reduce prediction loss relative to both no call and a call without its result. Fine-tuning on the augmented texts teaches tool use without downstream-task demonstrations. We fine-tune GPT-J with question answering, Wikipedia search, calculator, translation, and calendar APIs. Prompted zero-shot tests permit at most one call and trigger calls when their start token ranks among the ten most likely. On ASDiv, first-number accuracy is 40.4% with tools versus 14.8% with calls disabled and 14.0% for GPT-3 (175B); the enabled-disabled contrast shows that access to tools adds benefit beyond tool-annotated training. Factual completion, question answering, and temporal tasks improve over GPT-J baselines, including on the new template-generated DATESET. Question answering still trails GPT-3, while translation aids Toolformer without consistently surpassing original GPT-J. With calls disabled, language-modeling perplexity matches content-matched fine-tuning without API annotations. Three-tool scaling experiments place most tool benefits around 775M parameters, with search an exception. Chained and interactive tool use remain unsupported.
cases.notes: The loss filter supplies supervision for useful calls; the ASDiv enabled-disabled comparison distinguishes benefits of live tool access from gains already present after training. Table 3 uses first-number scoring (after '=' for equations), not complete-solution correctness, and GPT-3 is a larger, differently trained comparator. Retained DATESET, mixed QA/translation findings, and the content-matched, calls-disabled perplexity comparison. Section 4.4 scaling uses only three tools and exempts search; Section 6 bounds chained/interactive use. No temporal gain is attributed wholesale to the calendar.
